newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Polls close in Lithuania election, turn-out low.
newsitem.headline: Polls close in Lithuania election, turn-out low.

text.p: A low turn-out was reported on Sunday in the second round of Lithuania's parliamentary elections likely to usher independence leader Vytautas Landsbergis back to power.

The parliamentary press centre reported a 36.53 percent turn-out two hours before polls closed at 9 p.m. (19:00 GMT). This compared with 48.08 percent at the same time in the first round of the election on October 20.
Last month only 55 percent of eligible voters cast votes compared to around 75 percent in the the 1992 election, a year after Lithuania quit the Soviet Union.
Political analysts say Lithuanian voters, many of whom are struggling on a daily basis to make ends meet, are fed up with politics and preferred to spend their Sunday well away from polling stations.
Four years ago the Lithuanian electorate snubbed the Landsbergis government at the ballot box and voted in former communists, renamed the Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP).
It was a humiliating personal blow to the former music professor, who spearheaded his small nation's bid for independence after fifty years as an unwilling member of the Soviet Union.
That political shock started a regional trend of reformed communists being returned to power by voters reeling from the wrenching transition to capitalism.

The second round of the election works on a majority vote system with 65 seats up for grabs. Each seat is being contested by the two candidates who garnered the most votes in their electoral district for a total of 130 candidates.
Landsbergis and the board chairman of his Homeland Union party, Gediminas Vagnorius, each secured over 50 percent of the vote in their district in the first round.
Landsbergis is tipped to be chairman of the new parliament while Vagnorius will probably become the new prime minister.
The first round of the election last month allocated blocks in the 141-seat parliament to political parties on the basis of their share of the popular vote.
Landsbergis's Homeland Union triumphed in that round, gaining 33 of the 70 seats, while their future coalition partners, the Christian Democrats, got 11.
Both parties stress "traditional values" in the only former Soviet Republic where the majority of the populace is Roman Catholic.
The LDLP took 10, the populist Centre Union won nine on an anti-corruption and free market platform, while the Social Democrats scored seven seats.
The final results from Sunday's poll may not be known for several days.
